Annihilate

uh-NY-uh-layt -- from Latin ad- ('to') + nihil ('nothing') + -ate: literally 'to reduce to nothing.' · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To annihilate to destroy completely, often violently -- typically defeating an organized or living opponent so thoroughly that they cannot recover.

In the finals, the top-seeded chess prodigy annihilated her opponent, winning in under twenty moves.

Worked Example

In the championship debate, the returning state finalist dismantled every single one of her opponent's arguments point by point, leaving him with nothing left to say by the final round.

That kind of total, crushing defeat of a rival -- not just winning, but leaving them with nothing -- is exactly what it means to annihilate an opponent.

How Annihilate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

crush

crush: to defeat someone completely and decisively

vanquish

vanquish: to conquer or defeat thoroughly, especially in battle or competition

Antonyms

spare

spare: to refrain from harming or defeating someone

concede

concede: to admit defeat or give up a point to an opponent

How Strong Is It? — crush → annihilate → vanquish

crush vs. annihilate

crush vs. annihilate: Crush is a common, slightly informal word for a decisive win -- you can crush a rival team without necessarily wiping out every trace of their effort. Annihilate is stronger and more absolute, picturing total, overwhelming defeat with nothing left to fight back with.

vanquish vs. annihilate

vanquish vs. annihilate: Vanquish is close in strength to annihilate and shares its dramatic, almost historical tone -- both are usually reserved for a complete, decisive defeat of an enemy or rival, rather than a narrow win.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — an-

prefix — an-: to, toward (variant of Latin ad-)

root — -nihil-

root — -nihil-: nothing (Latin (nihil))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make, to cause to become (Latin (-are))

Put it together

Put it together: Annihilate comes from Latin ad- ('to') -- here spelled an- -- plus nihil ('nothing') plus -ate ('to make') -- so to annihilate something is literally to reduce it to nothing at all.

Use the root in a new word: nihilism

Use the root in a new word: nihilism: The philosophy professor spent the whole lecture explaining nihilism, the belief that life has no inherent meaning or value.

Root Check

Word Choice

Annihilate usually describes utterly defeating a living or organized opponent -- an army, a team, a debate rival -- unlike obliterate, taught earlier in this unit, which usually describes erasing a thing or a trace rather than defeating someone.
